title: Bhishma Waits for the Sun
hook: Bhishma, on a bed of arrows, waits for the sun to turn north: Hindus hold the turn sacred, and Ayurveda reads the same two halves in the body
carry: the sun's turn north is held sacred
tomorrow: why did the god of fire lose his appetite?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rama waited out the rains: the Hindu year has a season for waiting, and a season for going.

The greatest warrior of the Mahabharata has fallen. Bhishma, the old grandfather of both armies, lies on the battlefield held up by arrows, so many that his body doesn't touch the ground. He could die now. Long ago he was given a boon: he can choose his own time. And he chooses to wait. For the sun.
screen: `BHISHMA FALLS.` → `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `HE CHOOSES TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: Bhishma waits, the epic says, for many nights, until the sun turns north. While he waits, the Pandavas come to his bed of arrows, and he teaches them: the long talks of the Shanti book, on kingship, dharma and freedom. Then the sun turns, and he lets go. Uttarayana, the sun's northern course, is held as sacred time; the Gita names its six months among the signs of the path that leads to Brahman. Hindus celebrate the turn with Makar Sankranti in January: kites, sesame sweets, holy dips in rivers. Here's the teaching. Hindus see time itself as sacred, and the sun's two journeys, north and south, shape the religious year. Ayurveda reads the same sky in the body. The Charaka Samhita calls the northern half adana, the taking: the sun and the wind grow sharp and dry and draw strength out of the world and out of people. The southern half is visarga, the giving: the moon is strong, the earth is cooled by clouds and rain, and strength flows back. People are weakest, it says, where the taking ends and the giving begins, around the end of summer and the first rains. Today, that's a kinder way to read a low stretch. A drained late summer isn't a flaw in your character; on this lens, the year itself has a taking half. And Bhishma shows what a wait can hold: even on a bed of arrows, he used it to teach.
screen: `UTTARAYANA: THE SUN'S NORTHERN COURSE` · `MAKAR SANKRANTI MARKS THE TURN` · `ADANA TAKES, VISARGA GIVES` · `A LOW SEASON ISN'T A FAILING`

segments.voice: Many Hindus greet the morning sun with folded hands, some offering a little water toward it. Turn toward the light wherever you are, even a window, and fold your hands. Breathe out slowly, letting go of what this season has taken; breathe in, letting strength come back, with no forcing. If you pray, you can say Om Suryaya namah, a greeting to the sun; if you don't, simply feel the light.
The seasons. The sun's two courses: adana, the taking, while it goes north, and visarga, the giving, while it goes south.
Your line: the sun's turn north is held sacred. Bhishma waited for it. See you tomorrow.

adana.meaning: the taking: the half of the year when the sun goes north

visarga.meaning: the giving: the half of the year when the sun goes south

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (Bhishma falls onto a bed of arrows and resolves to wait for the sun's northern course); Shanti and Anushasana Parvas (his teaching to the Pandavas; his death when the sun turns north)
Bhagavad Gita 8.24 (fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course: those who depart then go to Brahman)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6.4–8 (the year in two halves, adana and visarga, with the sun's northern and southern courses; the qualities of sun, wind and moon in each; strength through the year)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 3.2–7 (uttarayana as adana, dakshinayana as visarga)
